newsitem.title: USA: Reducing risk in index funds.
newsitem.headline: Reducing risk in index funds.

text.p: Mutual funds that try to mimic the performance of a broad market index are enjoying a surge of popularity.
For example, assets invested in funds that track the Standard & Poor's 500 Index have grown from $3.8 billion in 1991 to more than $65 billion at the end of 1996.

That means there are a lot of satisfied investors out there. In recent years, the large-company stocks that make up the S&P 500 have been among the market's strongest performers. As a result, funds that track that index have outperformed most funds that attempt to add value by venturing outside of the index to invest in shares of small or mid-sized companies.
That performance has attracted billions of dollars to the index funds, which use the money to buy still more shares of the stocks that make up the S&P 500.

At the same time, many "active" money managers who can't afford to fall behind the overall market have shifted their assets into the stocks that make up the index. That process is known as "closet indexing." The result is that the index keeps rising, the funds post further gains and more investors are drawn to the funds ... and so on. In effect, the success of the funds is self-perpetuating.

But what happens when large-company stocks stumble? The S&P 500 and index funds that mimic it likely will lag more diversified funds that hold shares of smaller companies or overseas corporations. Investors will shift their money to those funds and market sectors, causing the S&P 500 to fall further behind -- and the index funds' success could rapidly unwind.

That scenario should not deter you from investing in index funds. Just make sure that your portfolio includes exposure to more than a single market sector. A number of funds invest in indices that are made up of shares of small, mid-sized and international companies, as well as bonds. Thus, you can use a mix of index funds to make sure your investments are well diversified.

Some investors shun index funds because such funds can't "beat the market." After all, they're just trying to match the performance of their chosen sector. With luck and skill, you might be able to outpace a portfolio of index funds by choosing winners for your fund portfolio.

For instance, an investor looking to put money to work in small-company stocks could own shares in Managers Special Equity (800-835-3879; $2,000 minimum investment; no load). The fund has gained 15.7 percent annually during the past 10 years, compared to 11 percent for the Russell 2000 index of small company stocks.

But such gains do carry additional risk. Even a fund that has a distinguished record might lag its benchmark index if the fund's approach falls from favor or its manager leaves. Moreover, not everyone wants to take the trouble to identify and monitor the most reliable funds in each sector. A portfolio of index funds is much simpler to manage, and helps to reduce the potential for surprises.

Moreover, index funds start the performance race with some built-in advantages. They have very low management costs because there's no need for an expensive team of stock pickers. And the funds' managers make few trades, so transaction costs are low as well. Annual stock index fund expenses typically are around 0.6 percent of assets vs. 1.5 percent for the average actively managed growth stock fund. Thus, shareholders get to keep more of the funds' profits.

If you're shopping for index funds, start with Vanguard, which has a wide selection of well-managed, efficiently run index funds. Their stock index fund offerings include Vanguard Index 500 (for all funds: 800-662-7447; $3,000 minimum; no load); Vanguard Index Small-Cap Stock, which attempts to mimic the performance of the Russell 2000 index of small company stocks; and Vanguard Index Extended Market, which tracks the Wilshire 4500 index of small and mid-sized company stocks.

Foreign stock fund investors can choose from four Vanguard entries that track indices: International Equity Index European; International Equity Index Pacific; and International Equity Index Emerging Markets. Or investors can pick Vanguard Total International Portfolio, which invests in the three international index funds mentioned above.
Vanguard also offers bond index funds such as Index Total Bond Market, which attempts to mirror the performance of the Lehman Brothers Aggregate Bond index.

Of course, there are plenty of other fund sponsors that offer index funds. One good choice is Schwab 1000 (800-526-8600; $1,000 minimum; no load), which invests in the 1,000 largest publicly traded U.S. companies. The fund has delivered a 37 percent higher return than its typical competitor during the past five years, with about 23 percent less volatility.
Another solid index fund is Dreyfus Mid-Cap Index (800-645-6561; $2,500 minimum; no load), which attempts to track the performance of the S&P MidCap 400 index of medium-sized U.S. firms.
(EDITORS: Clint Willis is a free-lance writer who covers financial issues for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Willis.)
